name: Water Spinach
variety: Species-level water spinach; no red/white biotype or named selection assigned
summary: Ipomoea aquatica is a warm-climate edible green with trailing, hollow stems and a serious aquatic-spread risk. UGA documents enclosed greenhouse DWC trials and soil high-tunnel production, but also notes invasive behavior and state-specific restrictions; check current local law and never release plant fragments or seed into waterways.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ipomoea aquatica. UGA Extension uses water spinach, kang kong, water convolvulus and swamp morning-glory; it describes red and white phenotypes but this identity does not select either phenotype.

growth.short: Trailing or floating hollow stems root at nodes
growth.guidance: UGA describes long hollow stems that may trail or float, with adventitious roots forming at nodes. The source says annual/perennial behavior depends on climate; this profile does not set a fixed life cycle independent of growing region.

cultivation.short: Heat-loving crop; UGA documents tightly contained production
cultivation.guidance: The UGA trials used greenhouse deep-water/pond culture or enclosed high tunnels, citing environmental spread risk. Warm conditions and full sun are described; open-water or escaped-fragment cultivation is not recommended. The study demonstrates a specific hydroponic research setting, not a general Garden nutrient recipe or legal permission.

harvest.short: Harvest shoots and retain basal growth for regrowth
harvest.guidance: In the UGA high-tunnel trials, shoots were cut while leaving basal leaves for regrowth; multiple harvests were documented. Timing and yield varied by site and planting date, so the study schedule is not generalized to every climate or cultivar.

propagation.short: Seed and node-rooting stem fragments are documented
propagation.guidance: UGA documents production from seed and rooting from stem nodes. Seed production and floating stem fragments create an ecological escape pathway; comply with current local regulation and contain all material. The cited Georgia article explicitly says cultivation was not permitted there at publication time.

problems.short: Containment and legal status are essential
problems.guidance: UGA reports naturalization in parts of the United States, identifies water spinach as a noxious weed in cited federal material, and describes Georgia restrictions at publication. These legal details are jurisdiction- and date-specific; verify current local rules before obtaining or growing it. Do not discard viable fragments or seed in drains, streams, ponds, or wetlands.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: UGA documents enclosed research trials using deep-water/pond culture, but this does not establish compatibility with Garden systems or transferable nutrient settings; calculator mapping remains insufficient.

evidence.note: Long trailing or floating stems root at nodes.

height.reason: The UGA article reports harvest shoot height in field trials, not a general mature-plant height.

spread.reason: The species can spread by floating fragments; no bounded mature spread is appropriate.

spacing.reason: UGA reports field-trial spacings that are not equivalent to container or pod spacing.

evidence.note: The source describes full sun for warm-climate production; not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Black Currant
summary: Ribes nigrum is the European black currant. University of Minnesota Extension describes a cool-climate fruiting shrub with cultivar-dependent self-fertility, annual cane renewal and regional white-pine-blister-rust considerations; no named cultivar is assigned.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ribes nigrum. The profile is species-level; extension cultivar names and their rust resistance or self-fertility are not generalized to an unspecified plant.

growth.short: Perennial fruiting shrub with multi-year canes
growth.guidance: UMN treats black currant as a woody perennial shrub. Fruit is borne on canes of different ages; the guide recommends retaining a balanced age structure when pruning established plants.

cultivation.short: Full sun to partial shade; richer sites support better fruiting
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension says currants grow in full sun to partial shade, with more fruit in full sun, and perform best in rich, well-drained soil. Its advice is scoped to Upper Midwest home gardens; local climate and rust regulations may differ.

maintenance.short: Prune canes annually and check local rust restrictions
maintenance.guidance: UMN recommends annual pruning to remove weak/dead canes and open the canopy. White pine blister rust restrictions apply in some US areas; consult current local rules and select cultivars with documented resistance where relevant.

harvest.short: Harvest when berries are purple-black and ripe
harvest.guidance: UMN notes ripe black currants develop a deep purple-black color and documents culinary use of the berries; it also notes leaves may be dried for tea. This is species/crop guidance, not a named cultivar harvest calendar.

propagation.short: Tip layering is documented; seed protocol is not established here
propagation.guidance: UMN notes that low, drooping canes can be covered to encourage rooting. The source does not provide seed-germination instructions, so no Seed Profile is assigned.

problems.short: White pine blister rust rules vary by location
problems.guidance: Ribes can participate in the white pine blister rust disease cycle, which may affect white pines; UMN states some areas retain planting restrictions. The warning is regional, not a universal prohibition.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The extension source concerns outdoor fruiting shrubs in soil, not hydroponic culture.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility schema has no woody-shrub category; the Plant Profile describes shrub form without forcing a narrower growth-habit mapping.

height.reason: No species-wide mature dimensions were selected from the cited extension article.

spread.reason: No species-wide mature dimensions were selected from the cited extension article.

spacing.reason: UMN gives field/garden shrub spacing; it is not a container or Garden-system placement recommendation.

light.reason: Outdoor exposure guidance is not converted to an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Red Currant
variety: Red currant horticultural form; no cultivar specified
summary: Ribes rubrum is an accepted currant species used for red, pink and white currant cultivars. Kew treats Ribes sativum as a synonym; University of Minnesota Extension describes the red/pink/white fruit forms as one species, not separate species identities.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ribes rubrum and treats Ribes sativum as a synonym. UMN uses Ribes sativum for red, pink and white currants and says these are the same species; this identity represents the species/crop, not an unnamed color cultivar.

growth.short: Woody currant shrub with berries in clusters
growth.guidance: UMN distinguishes currants from gooseberries by their spineless canes and clusters of small berries. This profile covers Ribes rubrum and does not claim that all commercial redcurrant cultivars share identical traits.

cultivation.short: Full sun to partial shade; fruiting improves in sunnier sites
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension states currants grow in full sun to partial shade, with greater fruiting in full sun, and prefer rich, well-drained soil. These recommendations are presented in Upper Midwest context.

maintenance.short: Renew older canes and keep the canopy open
maintenance.guidance: UMN recommends annual pruning to remove weak or dead canes and open the canopy. Rust restrictions and cultivar resistance vary by place and named selection.

harvest.short: Pick after fruit color and flavor develop
harvest.guidance: UMN recommends judging currants by color, flavor, firmness and ease of separation. Red, pink and white are horticultural fruit-color forms within the described species, not separate identities here.

propagation.short: Tip layering is mentioned; seed starting is not documented
propagation.guidance: UMN notes that drooping canes may be covered to encourage rooting. The page does not establish a seed-starting protocol for this identity, so none is invented.

problems.short: Check regional white pine blister rust restrictions
problems.guidance: UMN notes that Ribes can participate in the white pine blister rust cycle and that planting remains restricted in some US areas. This is jurisdiction-specific and should be checked locally.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited information concerns outdoor fruit shrubs in soil, not hydroponic production.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility schema has no woody-shrub category; shrub and cane structure remain described in the Plant Profile.

height.reason: The selected source does not provide species-wide dimensions for this profile.

spread.reason: The selected source does not provide species-wide dimensions for this profile.

spacing.reason: Garden shrub spacing is not converted into container/system placement.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor grow-light category.

name: European Gooseberry
variety: European species; American gooseberry hybrids are not included
summary: Ribes uva-crispa is the accepted European gooseberry species. UMN Extension distinguishes it from American gooseberries (Ribes hirtellum) and their hybrids; its cane pruning, fruit color and regional rust advice is home-garden guidance for the Upper Midwest.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ribes uva-crispa and lists Ribes grossularia among synonyms. UMN distinguishes this European species from American R. hirtellum and hybrids; no cultivar is assigned.

growth.short: Spiny woody shrub bearing individual berries
growth.guidance: UMN describes gooseberry canes as normally bearing a spine at each leaf node, with grape-sized berries singly or in small groups. These traits distinguish the crop from currants; individual cultivar traits are not implied.

cultivation.short: Full sun to partial shade in rich, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension says gooseberries grow from full sun to partial shade and perform best in rich, well-drained soil. Its recommendations are scoped to the Upper Midwest and may not transfer unchanged to other climates.

maintenance.short: Prune canes yearly and prevent ground-contact layering
maintenance.guidance: UMN recommends annual pruning to open the canopy and remove weak/dead canes. Gooseberry canes arching toward the soil may root at the tips; prune/manage them if that spread is not desired.

harvest.short: Pick as berries change color and soften
harvest.guidance: UMN says gooseberries are ready when they change color, become less firm and separate easily; ripening reduces tartness. Color depends on variety and is not a universal single-color maturity marker.

propagation.short: Tip layering is described; no seed protocol is supplied
propagation.guidance: UMN notes gooseberry cane tips can root where they touch soil. The cited page does not provide seed germination guidance, so this public profile does not invent a seed method.

problems.short: Check local white pine blister rust restrictions
problems.guidance: UMN notes some areas restrict Ribes due to white pine blister rust; it recommends varieties with known resistance where locally relevant. This is regional regulation/advice, not a universal restriction or blanket resistance claim.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The referenced guidance is for outdoor fruit shrubs in soil, not hydroponic production.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility schema has no woody-shrub category; Plant Profile keeps the evidence-backed shrub description.
